title: Links need text that says where they go
summary: A link has no text or accessible name, often an icon-only link. Add visible text or an aria-label that says where the link goes.
problem: An <a> element with an href has no text, no image with alt text and no aria-label. A typical case is a link around an icon, such as a cart or social media logo, where nothing tells assistive technology the destination.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users often browse by listing every link on a page. An unnamed link shows up as "link" or as the raw address, so they cannot pick the right one. Voice control users also cannot say a name to follow it.
whyItMatters: Links are how people move around a site. An unnamed link fails WCAG 4.1.2 at Level A and also WCAG 2.4.4 (Link Purpose in Context) at Level A, since its purpose cannot be worked out.
steps: Find the link in the scan result and see where it points.
Add text that names the destination, such as "View cart". Visible text helps everyone.
If the link must show only an icon, add aria-label to the link, such as aria-label="View cart", and set aria-hidden="true" on the icon.
If the link wraps an , give the image an alt that describes the destination, not the picture.
Avoid names like "click here" that make no sense out of context.
howToCheck: Select the link in the browser accessibility inspector and read its Name. An empty Name means the link is unnamed. A screen reader's links list should show a clear name for every entry.
